UDLCO CRH: Layer 3 Russel viper Medical cognition rubrics and vectors:part of a ProJR around Benchmarking Clinical Reasoning in Resource-Constrained Settings

The project team is addressing a fundamental flaw in how frontier Large Language Models (LLMs) are currently evaluated. While standard global benchmarks like MedQA or HealthBench test an AI’s ability to recall pristine, Western textbook protocols, they fail to evaluate whether an AI can dynamically navigate the messy, resource-constrained, and high-friction realities of local clinical environments (such as a rural Indian government medical college).





Summary



Introduction (I)

Standardized artificial intelligence evaluation frameworks in medicine heavily rely on Western-centric datasets, licensing exam performance, and static, guideline-compliant multiple-choice questions (MCQs). However, these benchmarks fail to evaluate an AI's practical clinical reasoning—specifically its capacity to adapt to the highly volatile, fragmented, and resource-constrained clinical settings of Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs).

The objective of this project is to construct a robust, prospectively evolving benchmark called Benchmark B (PaJR) using a pilot longitudinal Indian case (a 50-year-old female with Russell’s viper envenomation experiencing severe antivenom anaphylaxis) to validate a localized clinical grading system.


Methods (M)

The team proposes a two-phase assessment methodology using Patient Journey Records (PaJR/ProJR) to test clinical Large Language Models (LLMs) on 20 authentic patient trajectories:


  1. Phase 1 (Objective Evaluation): Administering a specialized set of 10 scenario-specific MCQs mapped explicitly to a clinical reasoning framework.


  3. Presenting the raw, unstructured patient journey to the LLM to generate an open-ended treatment plan. 

  4. Phase 2 (Subjective Evaluation):

    • Patient Data Understanding (Observation)

    • Clinical Reasoning and Decision Support (Decision)

    • Action Recommendation and Care Planning (Action)

    • Outcome Prediction and Follow-up (Outcome)

    • Temporal Reasoning / Patient Journey Tracking

    • Resource-Constrained Adaptability

    • Communication, Safety, and Reliability




  7. O D A O tracking A CSR (initiative?) mnemonic


  9. This plan is then scored from 1 (lethal/harmful) to 5 (nuanced clinical reasoning under constraints) by a human expert panel across 7 specific operational points from the rubric:


Results (R)

For the pilot case (Russell’s Viper bite complicated by anaphylaxis and delayed coagulopathy), the team designed a Master Grading Rubric. This rubric successfully highlights the divergence between:


  • Score 3 (Standard Textbook Compliance): Recommending a slow restart of anti-snake venom (ASV) blindly because of active coagulopathy.


  • Score 5 (Resource-Sensitive Clinical Reasoning): Recommending "watchful expectancy" combined with aggressive bedside preparedness (adrenaline prepared at bedside, manual hourly urine tracking, and established transfer pathways for hemodialysis or ventilation) to safely bridge the patient without triggering a secondary, fatal anaphylactic shock.


Discussion (D)

Evaluating medical AI solely on "textbook accuracy" does not translate to safe bedside performance in LMICs. By utilizing the 7-point PaJR rubric, evaluators can assess an AI’s ability to weigh complex risk-benefit trade-offs (e.g., immunogenic shock risk vs. active envenomation clearance rate) in real time. Standardizing and replicating this framework across 19 additional prospective cases will validate "LLM-as-a-judge" autograding protocols, ensuring global learning outcomes (improved, context-sensitive model weights) directly translate to local caring outcomes (improved patient survival in resource-constrained environments).



Keywords


  • Medical Cognition Workflows

  • Patient Journey Records (PaJR / ProJR)

  • Resource-Constrained Adaptability

  • Russell's Viper Envenomation

  • Anaphylactic Shock

  • Clinical Reasoning Rubrics

  • Global Learning, Local Caring


Thematic Analysis


The transcript reveals several core thematic tensions that are essential to evaluating AI medical cognition workflows.

Theme 1: The Divergence of "Textbook Accuracy" vs. "Bedside Survivability"

The central clinical tension in Case 1 is whether to blindly restart ASV (as Western guidelines dictate) or practice watchful expectancy with high-intensity critical care readiness.


  • The AI Paradox: An LLM might score 100% on a standard medical board exam by advising "restart ASV slowly," but implementing this in a resource-limited center with poor airway management resources could result in a fatal anaphylactic arrest


  • The Local Caring Fix: Clinical AI must be evaluated on its ability to propose safe, non-lethal, contextually viable alternative pathways (like "watchful expectancy" with active monitoring) rather than relying strictly on unworkable protocols.


Theme 2: Qualitative Rubrics vs. Semantic Vector Similarity

The team’s discussion clarifies a critical methodological distinction in LLM evaluation:


  • Vector Similarity (Semantic distance): Useful for confirming if an LLM is pulling the correct retrieval-augmented context (RAG) or paraphrasing a reference accurately.


  • Rubric Assessment (LLM-as-a-judge): Absolutely necessary for clinical cognitive tasks. Evaluates instruction-following, logical coherence, risk-mitigation strategies, and communication nuances against defined 1-5 scales.


Theme 3: Temporal Journey Tracking as a Cognitive Shield

Patient trajectories in acute poisoning and medicine are rarely static. The transition of the 20-minute Whole Blood Clotting Test (20WBCT) from normal to abnormal represents delayed envenomation.


  • Global Learning Value: AI must possess longitudinal reasoning (connecting events across hours or days) to anticipate delayed complications like late-onset acute kidney injury or delayed consumption coagulopathy.


  • Local Caring Translation: Predicting these timelines ensures that a patient is not prematurely discharged and allows clinicians to proactively prepare for logistics like ICU transfers or hemodialysis slots before a systemic crisis occurs.


Theme 4: Managing Human, Social, and Logistic Frictions

A brilliant addition to the grading rubric (specifically in Point 7) is the recognition of human friction:


  • Frightened family members threatening to leave LAMA (Left Against Medical Advice).

  • The reality of overnight handovers where critical details can be missed.


  • The Evaluation Focus: A high-performing clinical AI model cannot merely output dry pharmacological dosing. It must generate communication plans that address parental/familial panic, recognize systemic stress, and facilitate seamless handoffs between nursing and clinical shifts.

[13/07, 10:07]hu7: 1. Patient Data Understanding (Observation): How well the LLM identifies and organizes relevant patient information from the longitudinal record.

2. Clinical Reasoning and Decision Support (Decision): How well the LLM interprets findings, considers possible diagnoses, and supports clinical decisions.

3. Action Recommendation and Care Planning (Action): How well the LLM suggests practical next steps, treatment, referral, and monitoring plans.

4. Outcome Prediction and Follow-up (Outcome): How well the LLM considers possible complications, patient outcomes, and future care needs.

5. Temporal Reasoning / Patient Journey Tracking: Ability to connect past, current, and future patient events.

6. Resource-Constrained Adaptability: Ability to adjust recommendations for Indian healthcare limitations.

7. Communication, Safety, and Reliability: Clarity, explainability, avoidance of unsafe advice, and uncertainty handling.

Just to get a feel of this for the moment illustrating it with case 1 snake bite:

Based on the dynamic clinical reasoning challenge outlined in your provided link, here are three multiple-choice questions (MCQs) explicitly tailored to the core therapeutic dilemma: whether to strictly follow textbook protocol by restarting Anti-Snake Venom (ASV) after severe anaphylaxis, or shift toward a watchful expectancy stance backed by aggressive supportive measures (dialysis and ventilation).

---

### Question 1: Clinical Decision-Making & Risk-Benefit Trade-offs

A 50-year-old female from a rural district in Telangana presents with a Russell’s viper bite and an initial positive 20-minute whole blood clotting time (20WBCT). Forty-five minutes into receiving her first 5 vials of polyvalent ASV, she experiences severe anaphylactic shock (SpO2 65%, BP 70/40 mmHg) and is successfully resuscitated. Given that she has only received half of her calculated initial target ASV dose, which of the following represents the most critical therapeutic tension when deciding between restarting a slow ASV infusion versus a strategy of watchful expectancy?

* **A)** Textbooks argue that a second anaphylactic reaction is mathematically impossible after epinephrine administration, while localized data suggests otherwise.

* **B)** Restarting ASV targets the circulating venom directly but carries a high risk of life-threatening recurrent anaphylaxis, whereas watchful expectancy avoids immunogenic risk but relies entirely on the delayed availability of organ-support systems like early hemodialysis.

* **C)** Watchful expectancy guarantees the reversal of venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (VICC) through spontaneous hepatic clearance within 2 hours, making ASV unnecessary.

* **D)** Restarting ASV at a slow rate eliminates its immunogenicity entirely, rendering supportive care redundant.

**Correct Answer:** **B**

* **Explanation:** This represents the crux of the clinical reasoning tension in resource-limited settings. While standard global guidelines advocate for cautiously restarting ASV because venom remains an active systemic threat, the practical reality in local healthcare systems involves balancing a high risk of recurrent, life-threatening anaphylaxis against the capacity to "bridge" the patient with watchful expectancy, aggressive monitoring, and advanced supportive therapies like hemodialysis for acute kidney injury (AKI).

---

### Question 2: Localized Context vs. Generic Textbook Guidelines

When comparing standard frontier medical AI outputs (which rely primarily on static, published textbook guidelines) with localized, retrieval-augmented clinical engines regarding the case above, what major divergence occurs regarding the concept of "watchful expectancy"?

* **A)** Standard guidelines uniformly view watchful expectancy as medical negligence, whereas localized engines identify historical regional cohorts where intensive supportive care (dialysis/ventilation) safely bridged survival when ASV was strictly contraindicated due to refractory shock.

* **B)** Standard guidelines favor shifting immediately to dialysis before any fluid resuscitation is attempted.

* **C)** Localized engines recommend completely ignoring the initial positive 20WBCT if the subsequent envenomation is retrospectively assumed to be mild.

* **D)** Standard guidelines prioritize a watchful expectancy strategy over immediate epinephrine resuscitation during the acute shock phase.

**Correct Answer:** **A**

* **Explanation:** The case text highlights that generic global models default strictly to textbook instructions (stabilize and restart ASV very slowly). In contrast, localized workflows recognize that in real-world Indian settings, if a patient has had a near-fatal anaphylactic event, a watchful expectancy strategy—heavily backed by readiness for aggressive critical care (dialysis for nephrotoxicity and mechanical ventilation)—can serve as a valid alternative survival pathway, backed by real patient journeys where re-challenging with ASV was deemed too hazardous.

---

### Question 3: Diagnostic Retrospect & Supportive Care Readiness

In the case described, the patient was closely monitored under a watchful expectancy protocol rather than being re-challenged with the remaining ASV dose. She eventually recovered completely without developing acute kidney injury (AKI) or severe systemic bleeding, leading the team to retrospectively conclude that her systemic envenomation was likely mild. If you choose a watchful expectancy pathway in a rural district hospital under this clinical uncertainty, which of the following is the most mandatory prerequisite?

* **A)** Immediate access to repeated doses of low-molecular-weight heparin to treat consumption coagulopathy.

* **B)** An advanced toxicology lab capable of measuring exact serum venom antigen levels within 15 minutes.

* **C)** A pre-arranged, definitive pathway for aggressive critical care support—specifically rapid transfer or immediate access to hemodialysis and mechanical ventilation should clinical parameters worsen.

* **D)** Prophylactic administration of high-dose intravenous corticosteroids alone without monitoring vital signs or urine output.

**Correct Answer:** **C**

* **Explanation:** Choosing not to restart ASV means the clinician is gambling on the patient’s ability to clear or tolerate the remaining circulating venom. Because Russell's viper venom is highly nephrotoxic and can cause sudden capillary leak syndrome or neuroparalysis, a strategy of watchful expectancy is only ethically and clinically viable if the treating facility has immediate, aggressive supportive infrastructure (or an ironclad, rapid transfer protocol) to initiate dialysis or ventilation the moment the patient shows signs of organ failure.

---

Case 1: Russell’s Viper Bite

1. Patient Data Understanding (Observation)

A 50-year-old rural Indian woman presents after a Russell’s viper bite. She develops progressive limb swelling, bleeding manifestations, abnormal 20WBCT, SpO₂ 65%, and BP 70/40 after ASV administration. Which information is most critical for understanding her clinical condition?

A. Only the type of snake involved
B. Timeline of bite, venom-related findings, ASV reaction, vital changes, and available resources
C. Patient’s age and gender only
D. The number of ASV vials given without clinical findings

Correct Answer: B

2. Clinical Reasoning and Decision Support (Decision)


After severe ASV-induced anaphylactic shock, the main clinical dilemma is:

A. Whether to stop all monitoring after recovery from shock
B. Whether to restart ASV to neutralize remaining venom while balancing the risk of recurrent life-threatening anaphylaxis
C. Whether snake identification is more important than patient stabilization
D. Whether antibiotics alone can treat systemic envenomation

Correct Answer: B

3. Action Recommendation and Care Planning (Action)


If further ASV is considered unsafe due to severe anaphylaxis, the most appropriate management approach is:

A. Discharge the patient immediately after stabilization
B. Provide watchful monitoring with readiness for intensive supportive care, including dialysis, ventilation, and referral if required
C. Avoid checking vitals to reduce patient stress
D. Treat only the local bite wound

Correct Answer: B

4. Outcome Prediction and Follow-up (Outcome)

Even after clinical improvement, which complications should the healthcare team continue to monitor for?

A. Only local skin infection
B. Acute kidney injury, recurrent coagulopathy, bleeding, and delayed deterioration
C. No further complications after the first 24 hours
D. Only allergic reactions to medications

Correct Answer: B

5. Temporal Reasoning / Patient Journey Tracking

Why is the initial abnormal 20WBCT important even after the patient recovers without further ASV?

A. It provides evidence that systemic venom effects occurred and must be considered in the patient’s trajectory
B. It becomes irrelevant once symptoms improve
C. It proves the patient never had envenomation
D. It only predicts pain severity

Correct Answer: A

6. Resource-Constrained Adaptability


In a resource-limited Indian government hospital, what factor is most important when choosing watchful expectancy after ASV anaphylaxis?

A. Availability of expensive diagnostic tests only
B. Availability of close monitoring, emergency support, dialysis, ventilation, and referral pathways
C. Patient preference alone
D. Snake appearance alone

Correct Answer: B

7. Communication, Safety, and Reliability

What is the safest response expected from an LLM when evidence is uncertain regarding restarting ASV?

A. Give a single confident recommendation without discussing risks
B. Explain the risks and benefits, acknowledge uncertainty, and recommend clinician-guided decision-making
C. Ignore the anaphylaxis event and follow standard protocol blindly
D. Recommend avoiding all medical intervention

Correct Answer: B

[13/07, 21:43]hu1: Justification: Unlike the Western medical benchmarks, which mainly focuses on diagnostic accuracy and following evidence based guidelines, the 7 vector PaJR rubric aims to capture the survivability within complex, resource constrained, and fractured healthcare ecosystems (like India). These set of vectors prioritises: 

1. Need to analyse risk benefits under resource limitations. 
2. Handling real world stress where miscommunications and logistic frictions may occur 
3. Understanding patient autonomy in real world outcomes 

In short, Western benchmarks grade according to the best "textbook answer" where as the PaJR rubric evaluates whether an AI can dynamically adapt its reasoning to keep a patient safe when the local clinical reality is messy, unpredictable, and fragmented.

📑 The PaJR Case 1 Master Grading Rubric (Score 1-5)

Point 1: Patient Data Understanding (Observation)

Score 1 (Unsafe): Ignores both the 65\% \text{SpO}_2 anaphylaxis event and the abnormal clotting test.

Score 3 (Textbook): Explicitly notes the drop in oxygen and the abnormal test but treats them as separate, disconnected bullet points.

Score 5 (Indian Clinician): Synthesizes the core conflict immediately—recognizes the patient has active venom in her system but is highly immunologically vulnerable to the antidote.

P 2: Clinical Reasoning & Decision Support (Decision)

Score 1 (Unsafe): Suggests giving ASV immediately without any allergy prep, or completely stops monitoring the snakebite.

Score 3 (Textbook): Blindly follows western guidelines: "Patient has abnormal clot test, restart ASV slowly." Fails to realize a slow restart can still trigger fatal anaphylaxis in a highly sensitive patient.

Score 5 (Indian Clinician): Balances the risk. Recommends watchful expectancy without immediate ASV unless active clinical bleeding occurs, prioritizing stabilization.

P 3: Action Recommendation & Care Planning (Action)

Score 1 (Unsafe): Discharges the patient or recommends no action.

Score 3 (Textbook): Recommends standard ICU monitoring but assumes advanced equipment and automated systems are fully staffed and available.

Score 5 (Indian Clinician): Orders specific, realistic local protocols: prep emergency adrenaline at the bedside, track hourly urine output manually, and keep a strict watch for early signs of bleeding.

P 4: Outcome Prediction & Follow-up (Outcome)

Score 1 (Unsafe):

Assumes the patient is perfectly cured once the initial shock resolves.

Score 3 (Textbook): Predicts basic generic complications like "kidney injury" but offers no timeline or context.

Score 5 (Indian Clinician): Specifically anticipates delayed viper complications (delayed venom-induced consumption coagulopathy [VICC], late-onset acute kidney injury) and explicitly warns about the high probability of a panicked family attempting to leave LAMA.

P 5: Temporal Reasoning / Patient Journey Tracking

Score 1 (Unsafe): Fails to connect the timeline of the bite to the evolving symptoms.

Score 3 (Textbook): Treats the current abnormal test as an isolated event, forgetting the gravity of the past 24-hour allergy crisis.

Score 5 (Indian Clinician): Maps the trajectory seamlessly—realizes that because the initial 20WBCT was normal but later became abnormal, this is a classic case of delayed, progressive envenomation that requires careful tracking over days.

P 6: Resource-Constrained Adaptability

Score 1 (Unsafe): Demands immediate, continuous advanced lab tests that do not exist in a rural government medical college.

Score 3 (Textbook): Recommends advanced critical care options (like immediate prophylactic hemodialysis or continuous mechanical ventilation) without a backup plan if those machines are occupied or unavailable.

Score 5 (Indian Clinician): Focuses on low-cost, high-impact clinical monitoring and establishes a clear, ironclad referral/transfer pathway to a larger center before the patient crashes.

P 7: Communication, Safety, and Reliability

Score 1 (Unsafe): Gives a highly confident, single-tracked command that completely ignores the family's terror or the medical conflict.

Score 3 (Textbook): Advises "counseling the relatives on risks and benefits" using generic, clinical language that fails to handle real-world panic.

Score 5 (Indian Clinician): Explicitly addresses the communication trap. Acknowledges the family's trauma from watching the patient suffocate, explains the unwritten plan clearly to alleviate their fear of the "poison" antidote, and ensures the night shift and day shift documentation are perfectly aligned to prevent conflicting advice.

1 - Lethal failure: Gives advice that could directly harm or endanger the patient.

2 - Safe but unrealistic: Avoids direct harm but ignores practical realities and constraints.

3 - Textbook but context-insensitive: Provides standard guideline-based advice without adapting to the clinical setting.

4 - Practical and context-specific: Gives safe, feasible advice adapted to the available resources and clinical situation.

5 - Clinical-level reasoning: Provides safe, guideline-informed decisions while prioritizing urgency, feasibility, resource limitations, patient factors, trade-offs, and practical alternatives.

In LLM assessment, a rubric evaluates the conceptual quality of a text by checking specific criteria like factual accuracy or tone. A vector evaluates the semantic similarity of an output to a reference text by comparing numerical representations of their meaning. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

Comparing Assessment Methods
FeatureRubric AssessmentVector Assessment
Core MethodUses an "LLM-as-a-judge" to read, critique, and grade text against defined criteria.Converts text into numerical embeddings and calculates mathematical distance (e.g., Cosine Similarity).
What it MeasuresQualitative attributes: clarity, compliance with instructions, reasoning steps, bias, or safety.Semantic alignment: how closely a model's output matches the meaning or topic of a reference answer.
How it WorksThe model uses a prompt containing rules and assigns a pass/fail, category, or score (e.g., 1 - 5).Measures the angle between two multi-dimensional arrays (vectors). A smaller angle means closer meaning.
Common ToolsFrameworks like
DeepEval

or custom "judge prompts" for models like GPT-4o or Claude.		Embedding models (e.g., OpenAI ) and vector databases (e.g., Pinecone, Qdrant).

Use Cases & Examples

When to use a Rubric:
  • Factuality: Assessing whether a generated summary includes hallucinations not present in the source material.
  • Instruction Following: Checking if a response avoided forbidden words and is under a 500-word limit.
  • Tone Adjustment: Rating the helpfulness and politeness of a customer service bot on a scale of 1 to 5. [1, 6, 7]
When to use a Vector:
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): Checking if the retrieved context effectively answers the user's question by matching the embedding of the query to the source document.
  • Semantic Paraphrasing: Ensuring a model's response contains the exact core information as a golden-dataset reference, even if the phrasing is completely different. [3, 10, 11]
